# Review

# Mobile Apps

## React Native
React Native is a framework for building *cross-platform* mobile apps.

A framework is a set of tools and libraries that make it easier to build software.

## Expo
Expo is also a framework, but its focus is on:

- Automating the build, test, and deployment process
- Sharing code between platforms (e.g. Android and iOS)
- Providing a simulation environment

## TypeScript
TypeScript is JavaScript but with types (like in C).

<br>

Files ending in `.tsx` are TypeScript files.

<br>

React Native uses TypeScript by default.

## Getting Started

In a terminal:
```{.zsh code-line-numbers="false"}
# Install Expo CLI globally
npm install -g expo-cli

# Create a new project
npx create-expo-app MyFirstApp

# Navigate to project folder
cd MyFirstApp

# Start the development server
npx expo start
```

Expo creates a React Native project for you

::: {.notes}
demo how to open on the simulator and on the phone
:::

## Components
Components are like lego pieces that you can combine to build a mobile app.

<br>

The [root]{.highlight-red} component is the `App` function by default or the `index.js` file.

<br>

Everything else starts from the [root]{.highlight-red} component.

::: {.notes}
go over the project folder
:::

## Creating Components {auto-animate="true"}

Create components using HTML and other components.

```{.jsx filename="index.tsx" code-line-numbers=3-11|13-21}
import { Text, TouchableOpacity, View } from "react-native";

function Greeting({ name }: { name: string }) {
  // name is a prop (aka parameter)
  return (
    // Curly braces interpolate the value of `name` into the text
    <View>
      <Text>Hello, {name}!</Text>
    </View>
  );
}

export default function App() {
  return (
    <View>
      <TouchableOpacity>
        <Text>Press Me</Text>
      </TouchableOpacity>
    </View>
  );
}
```

::: {.notes}
explain props
:::

## Creating Components {auto-animate="true"}

We can then use this component in our `App` component.

```{.jsx filename="index.tsx" code-line-numbers=11-21}
function Greeting({ name }: { name: string }) {

  return (
    // Curly braces interpolate the value of `name` into the text
    <View>
      <Text>Hello, {name}!</Text>
    </View>
  );
}

export default function App() {
  return (
    <View>
      <Greeting name="Sarah" />
      <Greeting name="Mike" />
      <TouchableOpacity>
        <Text>Press Me</Text>
      </TouchableOpacity>
    </View>
  );
}
```

## Built-In Components

React Native provides a set of built-in components that you are encouraged to use.

- View
- Text
- TouchableOpacity
- Image
- FlatList
- ... and more

## Styling Components {auto-animate="true"}

Create a `StyleSheet` object to define CSS-like styles.

```{.jsx filename="index.tsx" code-line-numbers=21-52|25-30|3-19}
import { StyleSheet, Text, TouchableOpacity, View } from "react-native";

function Greeting({ name }: { name: string }) {
  return (
    <View>
      <Text>Hello, {name}!</Text>
    </View>
  );
}

export default function App() {
  return (
    <View>
      <Greeting name="Sarah" />
      <Greeting name="Mike" />
      <TouchableOpacity>
        <Text>Press Me</Text>
      </TouchableOpacity>
    </View>
  );
}

const styles = StyleSheet.create({
  // This is CSS-like styling
  container: { // Class name
    flex: 1,
    justifyContent: 'center',
    alignItems: 'center',
    backgroundColor: '#fff',
  },
  greetingContainer: {
    marginVertical: 10,
    padding: 15,
    backgroundColor: '#e0e0e0',
    borderRadius: 8,
  },
  greetingText: {
    fontSize: 18,
    color: '#333',
  },
  button: {
    marginTop: 20,
    backgroundColor: '#007AFF',
    padding: 12,
    borderRadius: 8,
  },
  buttonText: {
    color: 'white',
    fontSize: 16,
    fontWeight: 'bold',
  },
});
```

## State

State lets a component “remember” information like user input (i.e. a variable for a component)

```{.jsx filename="CounterApp.tsx" code-line-numbers=|6-7|11|16}
import React, { useState } from 'react';
import { View, Text, TextInput, TouchableOpacity, StyleSheet } from 'react-native';

const CounterApp = () => {
  // useState returns [currentValue, setterFunction]
  const [count, setCount] = useState(0);
  const [name, setName] = useState('');

  return (
    <View style={styles.container}>
      <Text style={styles.title}>Counter: {count}</Text>

      <View style={styles.buttonRow}>
        <TouchableOpacity
          style={styles.button}
          onPress={() => setCount(count + 1)}
        >
          <Text style={styles.buttonText}>Increment</Text>
        </TouchableOpacity>

        <TouchableOpacity
          style={[styles.button, styles.resetButton]}
          onPress={() => setCount(0)}
        >
          <Text style={styles.buttonText}>Reset</Text>
        </TouchableOpacity>
      </View>

      <TextInput
        style={styles.input}
        placeholder="Enter your name"
        value={name}
        onChangeText={setName}
      />

      {name ? <Text>Hello, {name}!</Text> : null}
    </View>
  );
};

const styles = StyleSheet.create({
  container: { flex: 1, justifyContent: 'center', alignItems: 'center', padding: 20 },
  title: { fontSize: 24, fontWeight: 'bold', marginBottom: 20 },
  buttonRow: { flexDirection: 'row', marginBottom: 20 },
  button: { backgroundColor: '#007AFF', padding: 12, borderRadius: 8, marginHorizontal: 5 },
  resetButton: { backgroundColor: '#FF3B30' },
  buttonText: { color: 'white', fontSize: 16 },
  input: { borderWidth: 1, borderColor: '#ccc', padding: 10, borderRadius: 8, width: 200, marginBottom: 20 }
});

export default CounterApp;
```

## State Types
Instead of setting name to be an empty string by default, we can set it to null.

```{.jsx}
const [name, setName] = useState(null);
```

::: {.fragment .fade-in}
But now React doesn't know the type of name.
:::

## State Types
We can specify the type of name to be a string OR null.

```{.jsx}
const [name, setName] = useState<string | null>(null);
```

::: {.fragment .fade-in}
Now, later on we can set name to be a string.

```{.jsx}
setName("Nikki")
```

NOTE: there is no "integer" type, instead it's called "number" in typescript.
:::

::: {.notes}
- bar means or
:::

## Component Logic

Rendering code

- "pure" calculations, predictable results

Event handlers

- functions that *do* things, unpredictable, triggered by events (e.g. user input)

::: {.fragment .fade-in}
Effects

- a side effect caused by rendering (i.e. after rendering, what needs to be updated?)
:::

## Effects

React resolves effects after rendering the page or a specific dependency.

```{.jsx filename="DataFetcher.tsx" code-line-numbers=|5-7|9-39|}
import { useEffect, useState } from "react";
import { ActivityIndicator, StyleSheet, Text, View } from "react-native";

const DataFetcher = () => {
	const [data, setData] = useState<string | null>(null);
	const [loading, setLoading] = useState(true);
	const [error, setError] = useState<string | null>(null);

	useEffect(() => {
		// This runs after component mounts
		console.log("Component mounted - fetching data");

		const fetchData = async () => {
			try {
				// Simulating API call
				const response: { message: string } = await new Promise(
					(resolve) =>
						setTimeout(
							() => resolve({ message: "Hello from API!" }),
							2000,
						),
				);
				setData(response.message);
			} catch (err: any) {
				setError(err.message);
			} finally {
				setLoading(false);
			}
		};

		fetchData();

		// Cleanup function (runs before unmount or before next effect)
		return () => {
			console.log(
				"Cleanup - component unmounting or dependencies changed",
			);
		};
	}, []); // Empty array = runs only once on mount, add dependencies here if needed

	if (loading)
		return (
			<View style={styles.center}>
				<ActivityIndicator size="large" color="#007AFF" />
				<Text>Loading...</Text>
			</View>
		);

	if (error)
		return (
			<View style={styles.center}>
				<Text style={styles.error}>Error: {error}</Text>
			</View>
		);

	return (
		<View style={styles.center}>
			<Text>{data ? data : "No data available"}</Text>
		</View>
	);
};

const styles = StyleSheet.create({
	center: { flex: 1, justifyContent: "center", alignItems: "center" },
	error: { color: "red" },
});

export default DataFetcher;
```

::: {.notes}
walk through the componentn and ask them what kind of logic each part is
:::

# Tutorial

## Why is it Lossy?

### Range
BLE devices have a typical range less than 10 meters.

### Inteference
BLE operates on the 2.4 GHz frequency band, which is shared with other wireless technologies.

- ISM devices (e.g. microwave ovens, medical diathermy devices)
- WiFi
- Bluetooth

## Channel Hopping
A channel is a specific frequency channel in between 2.4 GHz and 2.5 GHz.

A BLE device constantly hops between channels to avoid interference.

![](./images/channel-hop.png){fig-align="center"}

::: {.notes}
advertising channels do not change
:::

## Packet Loss
Packet loss may occur whenever the device is too far or when there is interference.

<br>

The BLE device changes channels but any lossed packets need to be resent.
